items.prompt: Where on a growing shoot does it actually get longer?

options.label: Only at the very tip
options.feedback: A cluster of dividing cells at the tip keeps churning out new cells, and everything below simply stays as it was made.

options.label: Evenly along the whole shoot
options.feedback: Mark two points a hand's-width apart on a young shoot in spring and measure them again in autumn — the gap barely changes, because growth isn't spread out like that.

options.label: Only where the bark is thinnest
options.feedback: Bark thickness has nothing to do with where a shoot lengthens; a shoot inside thick bark can grow just as fast as one inside thin bark.

options.label: Only on the side facing the sun
options.feedback: A shoot can bend toward the sun, but the bending happens because growth at the tip is uneven, not because growth happens somewhere along the side.

items.ok_line: All the new length comes from one small patch of dividing cells.
items.ko_line: Growth in a shoot is concentrated, not smeared along its length.
items.exp_title: A shoot lengthens from one end only
items.exp_text: At the very tip of every growing shoot sits a cluster of constantly dividing cells called the apical meristem, and it is the only place producing brand-new cells for that shoot. Each new cell then stretches to something like its final length just behind the tip, and once it has stretched it stays fixed for the rest of its life. That is why a shoot gets longer by adding fresh material at its growing point, never by the older wood behind it stretching further.

items.prompt: If you hammer a nail into a tree trunk at chest height, why does it stay at the same height years later even as the tree grows taller?

options.label: The tree grows equally in every direction, so height and nail position move together
options.feedback: If growth happened equally everywhere the nail actually would climb with the tree — that's exactly why this isn't what happens.

options.label: Wood around the nail simply pushes it back out over time
options.feedback: The wood does grow thicker around the nail and can eventually swallow it, but that changes the nail's depth, not its height.

options.label: The tree stops growing taller once it reaches a certain age, so nothing moves
options.feedback: Even old, slow-growing trees keep adding a small amount of height most years; the nail's height staying fixed isn't about growth stopping.

options.label: All the new height is added at the branch tips above, not at the trunk below
options.feedback: The trunk where the nail sits was itself once a growing tip; once it hardened into wood, its height was fixed for good.

items.ok_line: The trunk you nailed into never moves; new trunk gets built on top of it.
items.ko_line: Ask where the tree is actually manufacturing new length, not where the nail sits.
items.exp_text: A trunk lengthens only at the growing tips of its branches, high above where the nail sits, so each year's new height is added on top of everything that came before. The section of trunk holding the nail was itself once a growing tip, but the moment it hardened into wood it stopped changing height forever. From then on it only ever gets thicker, never taller, which is why the nail keeps its place while the crown above climbs away from it.

items.prompt: What makes a tree trunk grow thicker year after year?

options.label: The centre of the trunk keeps expanding outward
options.feedback: The centre is the oldest, most rigid wood in the whole trunk; nothing there is still capable of expanding.

options.label: A thin layer under the bark keeps adding new wood and bark
options.feedback: Every bit of extra girth traces back to that one dividing layer.

options.label: Old wood cells slowly swell up over time
options.feedback: A wood cell reaches its size once and then stops; nothing about being older makes a cell bigger.

options.label: Rainwater absorbed into the wood makes it expand
options.feedback: Wood does hold water, and a very dry log shrinks slightly, but that's a small reversible change, not the steady growth that adds real girth year after year.

items.ok_line: All the trunk's growth in width comes from a sheet just under the bark.
items.ko_line: The part of the trunk doing the growing is a thin strip, not the bulk of it.
items.exp_title: A ring of dividing cells under the bark
items.exp_text: Just beneath the bark runs a thin layer called the cambium, a ring of cells that keeps dividing all the way around the trunk. Each division adds a new cell of wood on the inside and a new cell of bark on the outside, so the whole ring shifts slightly further from the centre every time it divides. Everything inside that ring — all the wood you see when a log is cut — was made this way, one thin layer added on top of the last.

items.prompt: Why does a cut tree trunk show alternating light and dark rings?

options.label: Each ring is a different wood chemical
options.feedback: It's the same wood tissue throughout; no different chemical is laid down ring by ring.

options.label: The rings mark old lightning strikes
options.feedback: A lightning strike leaves a scar in one spot on one side of the trunk, not a ring running all the way around it.

options.label: Spring cells grow large and pale, later cells grow small and dense
options.feedback: Two growth speeds inside one year leave two different textures behind.

options.label: Dark rings are dead wood and light rings are living wood
options.feedback: Every ring inside the trunk is dead wood by the time it's visible; only the thin cambium layer right under the bark is alive.

items.ok_line: Fast spring growth and slower late-season growth leave two different textures.
items.ko_line: The bands come from cell size and growth speed, not damage or chemistry.
items.exp_title: A record of the growing season
items.exp_text: In spring the cambium divides quickly and produces large, thin-walled cells built for moving lots of water, which look pale. As the season goes on, growth slows and the cambium switches to making smaller, thick-walled cells packed close together, which look dark. That shift from fast pale growth to slow dark growth happens once every year, so each light-dark pair traces one full cycle from a fast start to a slow finish.

items.prompt: Why does the bark of an old tree often look cracked and split into plates?

options.label: The wood underneath keeps expanding while the rigid outer bark cannot stretch to match
options.feedback: The outer bark is dead tissue; it can only tear as the living wood beneath it keeps pushing outward.

options.label: Bark is a living tissue that grows unevenly on its own
options.feedback: The living part of the bark sits right against the cambium; the cracked outer surface you see is dead tissue, not living cells growing unevenly.

options.label: Insects burrow patterns into the surface over many years
options.feedback: Insect tunnels do leave marks, but the wide cracking and plating of a whole trunk's surface happens on trees with no insect damage at all.

options.label: Sunlight dries and shrinks the outer surface unevenly
options.feedback: Sun does weather the outer surface, but a shaded trunk in a dense forest cracks and plates in exactly the same way.

items.ok_line: Wood underneath keeps growing while the outer skin can't keep up.
items.ko_title: The cause is inside, not outside
items.ko_line: Whatever is cracking the bark has to come from the trunk expanding, not from anything acting on the surface.
items.exp_text: The cambium keeps adding wood on the inside of the bark, so the trunk's circumference is constantly increasing. The living inner bark can stretch and divide to keep pace, but the tough, dead outer bark cannot — it can only tear. That tearing, repeated in the same places as the trunk keeps widening, is what turns a smooth young trunk into deep cracks and plates.

items.prompt: Why does cutting off the main growing tip of a young tree often make side branches sprout out lower down?

options.label: The tip was blocking sunlight from reaching the buds below
options.feedback: A slim growing tip casts almost no shade on the buds directly beneath it; blocking light isn't what was holding them back.

options.label: Removing the tip triggers the roots to send up more water
options.feedback: Roots don't respond to a cut tip by suddenly pumping more water; nothing about the water supply changes the moment the tip is removed.

options.label: The tree grows extra branches in reaction to the injury
options.feedback: There's no general injury response that sprouts branches anywhere on the tree; only the buds that were being held back by the tip start growing, and only once that hold is gone.

options.label: The tip was producing a hormone that suppressed the growth of buds below it
options.feedback: Cut the tip away and that suppressing signal stops reaching the buds beneath it.

items.ok_line: The tip was quietly holding every bud below it in check.
items.ko_title: Not light, not water, not injury
items.ko_line: Something chemical was suppressing those buds, and removing the tip removes it.
items.exp_title: The tip was holding everything else back
items.exp_text: The growing tip constantly produces a hormone that travels down the shoot and keeps the buds below it dormant, a control called apical dominance. Cut the tip away and the supply of that hormone stops reaching the buds beneath it. Freed from the signal that was holding them back, several of those buds start growing at once, which is why the tree fills out into a bushier shape.

items.prompt: What is a leaf bud, before it opens in spring?

options.label: A ball of stored sap waiting to be released
options.feedback: Sap does move through a bud once it opens, but the bud itself isn't a reservoir of liquid — it's solid tissue, tightly packed.

options.label: A tightly folded miniature shoot, already formed the year before
options.feedback: The leaves and stem for next spring were assembled the previous summer, then wrapped and set aside.

options.label: A seed that has attached itself to the branch
options.feedback: A seed comes from an entirely different part of the plant and would never be attached along a bare twig like this.

options.label: Dead tissue that softens and turns into a leaf
options.feedback: Nothing dead can turn into living leaf tissue; a bud is made of living cells from the moment it forms.

items.ok_line: The leaves and stem were assembled last year, waiting for spring.
items.ko_title: Not stored liquid, not dead tissue
items.ko_line: A bud is living structure, already shaped, just packed very small.
items.exp_text: By late summer a tree has already built the tiny leaves and stem segments it will need next spring, folded tightly together and wrapped in tough protective scales to form a bud. All winter that miniature shoot sits dormant, fully formed but not growing. When warmth returns, the scales fall away and the shoot simply unfolds and expands, rather than being built from scratch.

items.prompt: Why can an old tree with a completely hollow trunk still be alive and healthy?

options.label: The tree has rerouted all its water transport through the roots instead
options.feedback: There's no separate route through the roots that bypasses the trunk; water still has to travel up through trunk tissue, just not through the hollow part.

options.label: Hollow trunks are actually stronger than solid ones
options.feedback: A hollow tube can resist bending fairly well for its weight, but nobody would call a rotted-out trunk stronger than the solid wood it replaced.

options.label: The hollow centre was never doing a living job in the first place
options.feedback: The oldest wood at the centre stops carrying water and becomes purely structural years before it ever rots.

options.label: The rot inside somehow feeds the tree extra nutrients
options.feedback: Decay breaks wood down for the fungi and microbes doing the rotting, not for the tree — it's a loss to the tree, not a gain.

items.ok_line: The centre stopped doing anything useful long before it ever rotted.
items.ko_line: This is about what the centre was doing before the rot, not after.
items.exp_text: The oldest wood at the centre of a trunk, called heartwood, stops carrying water years before it ever rots — it becomes purely structural, holding the tree upright and nothing more. All of a tree's actual living, working tissue sits in a thin outer ring: the cambium, the young sapwood carrying water, and the bark. Fungi that rot out the heartwood are hollowing out a part the tree had already finished using, which lets the tree lose that whole core and carry on as before.

items.prompt: In a cut log, why is the newest wood found just under the bark rather than at the centre?

options.label: The cambium that produces new wood sits just inside the bark, and every layer it makes stays where it was made
options.feedback: Each new layer becomes, for a while, the outermost ring — until the next year's layer is added outside it in turn.

options.label: Wood fibres migrate outward over time as the tree ages
options.feedback: A wood cell never moves once it's formed; there's no mechanism carrying finished fibres from one spot to another inside solid wood.

options.label: Termites and insects hollow out the older wood in the middle first
options.feedback: Insect damage can hollow a trunk, but that's decay removing wood, not an explanation for where the newest layer sits in a healthy log.

options.label: The centre wood dissolves and reforms nearer the surface
options.feedback: Wood doesn't dissolve and reappear elsewhere; once a cell is built it stays exactly where the cambium made it, permanently.

items.ok_line: Every new ring is laid down right next to the bark, pushing the old rings inward.
items.ko_line: Wood cells are fixed for life the moment they're made — think about where the cambium actually sits.
items.exp_title: The growing edge is under the bark
items.exp_text: New wood is only ever made by the cambium, and the cambium sits in a fixed position just beneath the bark, never at the centre of the trunk. Each time it divides it adds a fresh cell to the wood side, and that fresh cell becomes part of the outermost ring of wood for the time being. Counting inward from the bark therefore takes you backward through time, toward the wood the tree grew before all the rest of it existed.

items.prompt: Why does the base of many tree trunks flare out wider just above ground level, even where the soil is undisturbed?

options.label: Water pools there and swells the wood
options.feedback: A tree base swollen by standing water would be a sign of trouble, not a normal healthy shape found on dry ground too.

options.label: Old bark simply piles up at the bottom over time
options.feedback: Bark doesn't accumulate or pile up; each layer stays where it grew, so this can't explain a change in shape.

options.label: Roots push the base outward as they grow underground
options.feedback: Roots do widen the spot where they join the trunk, but the smooth outward flare of the trunk itself is added by the trunk, not shoved out by roots below.

options.label: The trunk adds extra wood exactly where wind stress is greatest
options.feedback: The base takes the most bending force whenever the crown sways, and the cambium responds by building up material there.

items.ok_line: The trunk thickens exactly at the point taking the most strain.
items.ko_title: Not water, not bark, not push
items.ko_line: Think about which part of the trunk is under the most mechanical load when the crown sways.
items.exp_title: Wood laid down to match the strain
items.exp_text: When wind sways a tree's crown, the leverage of that whole weight concentrates its bending force at the base of the trunk, right where it meets the ground. A tree responds to that repeated strain by laying down extra wood exactly there, widening the base into a flare rather than growing evenly all the way down. The result is a trunk that keeps reinforcing exactly the spot where a swaying crown puts real strain on it.
